newsitem.title: UK: UK Referendum party becoming a force, Redwood says.
newsitem.headline: UK Referendum party becoming a force, Redwood says.

text.p: The anti-European Referendum party is becoming a serious political force that could cost the ruling Conservatives key marginal seats at Britain's looming election, right-wing Conservative John Redwood said on Sunday.

Redwood, a former cabinet minister, was commenting on the defection to the Referendum party of disaffected Conservative member of parliament Sir George Gardiner, who quit saying he could no longer stand Prime Minister John Major's equivocation on Europe.

Accusing Major of sitting on the fence, especially on whether to join the European Union's planned single currency, Gardiner wrote in the Sunday Times: "The cheeks of his bottom hold the top of the fence tightly in their grip."

Gardiner, an ardent Euro-sceptic opposed to closer European ties, had already been dropped by his local Conservative association as its candidate for the election due to an earlier jibe in which he likened Major to a ventriloquist's dummy.
But his defection to the Referendum party, founded and financed by billionaire Anglo-French entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith, is nevertheless another serious blow to Major.

Redwood, who failed in a challenge to Major's leadership of the Conservative party in July 1995, shares Gardiner's scepticism towards Europe but said the 62-year-old rebel was wrong to desert the Conservatives so close to the election, widely expected to take place on May 1.

"The only way George and I will get what we want -- which is a strong Britain in a strong Europe, but an independent self-governing Britain in the main -- is to elect a Conservative government and then to make sure that it doesn't give any more powers away to Europe," Redwood told Sky Television.
Opinion polls give the Referendum party, whose sole purpose is to force a plebiscite on Britain's ties with Europe, about two percent of the vote.

Although it has no chance of winning a seat, Redwood said this could be enough to tip the balance in marginal constituencies that might determine whether the main opposition Labour party seizes power from the Conservatives for the first time since 1979.
"That's why I'm worried about it and why I would urge all Conservatives not to support the Referendum party," he said.
"It's a serious force in British politics to the extent that I think it's going to influence the agenda of the election," Redwood added.
By reminding voters of the Conservatives' deep divisions over Europe, Gardiner's desertion was another gift to Labour, which has an opinion poll lead of about 20 points.

"What George Gardiner's defection shows is just further disintegration in the Tory party. This is a government that is simply limping to the finishing post, and the sooner we have a general election in this country, the better," Labour's health spokesman, Chris Smith, told BBC television.
Cabinet members put a brave face on the setback. "It doesn't alter the basic choice that faces people in the general election," Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell told the BBC.
Gardiner is the fourth MP to quit the Conservatives in the past 18 months. Two joined the minority Liberal Democrats and another went over to Labour.

His defection theoretically puts Major's government into a minority of three in the 651-seat House of Commons (lower house). But he can hang on thanks to support from the nine members of Northern Ireland's Ulster Unionist party.
